challenger.place: over the Atlantic Ocean, off Cape Canaveral, Florida
challenger.opening: On 28 January 1986, this happened to seven real people.

crew.name: Francis R. (Dick) Scobee
crew.line: He enlisted in the US Air Force and earned his aerospace engineering degree through night classes before becoming a pilot and then a shuttle commander.

crew.name: Michael J. Smith
crew.line: A US Navy test pilot who had logged more than 4,300 flight hours, he was making his first spaceflight.

crew.name: Ellison S. Onizuka
crew.line: Born in Kealakekua, Hawaii, he was the first Asian American to fly in space, and was on his second flight.

crew.name: Judith A. Resnik
crew.line: An electrical engineer with a doctorate, she was among the first women selected as NASA astronauts and became the second American woman in orbit.

crew.name: Ronald E. McNair
crew.line: A laser physicist with a doctorate from MIT, he was also a karate black belt and a saxophone player, and the second Black American in space.

crew.name: Gregory B. Jarvis
crew.line: An engineer at Hughes Aircraft, he was chosen to fly after competing against about 600 of his Hughes colleagues.

crew.name: S. Christa McAuliffe
crew.line: A high-school social studies teacher from Concord, New Hampshire, chosen from more than 11,000 applicants, she had planned to teach lessons from orbit, including one called "The Ultimate Field Trip".

happened: Challenger lifted off on a cold morning, and about 73 seconds later the vehicle broke apart.
The Rogers Commission found that the failure began at a joint in the right solid rocket booster, where hot gases escaped past damaged O-ring seals.
The commission also found that warnings about the joint and the cold had not been given enough weight in the decision to launch.
changed: President Reagan set up the Rogers Commission, which investigated the accident and made recommendations to NASA.
The solid rocket booster field joint was redesigned and tested with full-scale firings before flights resumed.
NASA added a crew escape system for some flight conditions and pressure suits for launch and entry.
NASA strengthened its safety oversight and management structure, and shuttle flights resumed with STS-26 on 29 September 1988, 32 months later.
challenger.lesson: Safety concerns raised by the people closest to the hardware must be heard and acted on, even when there is pressure to keep to the schedule.

quote.text: The crew of the space shuttle Challenger honored us by the manner in which they lived their lives.
quote.by: President Ronald Reagan, address to the nation, 28 January 1986

columbia.place: over Texas and Louisiana, during re-entry, about 16 minutes before the planned landing in Florida
columbia.opening: On 1 February 2003, this happened to seven real people.

crew.name: Rick D. Husband
crew.line: A US Air Force colonel and test pilot, he had piloted STS-96, the first shuttle mission to dock with the International Space Station.

crew.name: William C. McCool
crew.line: A US Navy commander and former test pilot, he was making his first spaceflight; his nickname was Willie.

crew.name: Michael P. Anderson
crew.line: An Air Force lieutenant colonel with a physics degree, he was in charge of the science mission aboard STS-107 and had flown to the Mir space station in 1998.

crew.name: David M. Brown
crew.line: He was both a US Navy aviator and a flight surgeon, flying in space for the first time.

crew.name: Kalpana Chawla
crew.line: Born in Karnal, India, she studied aeronautical engineering in Punjab, earned a doctorate in the United States and became the first woman of Indian origin to fly in space.

crew.name: Laurel B. Clark
crew.line: A Navy captain-select and flight surgeon, she was on her first spaceflight and worked on science experiments in the Spacehab module.

crew.name: Ilan Ramon
crew.line: A colonel and fighter pilot in the Israeli Air Force, he was Israel's first astronaut, and carried a replica of 'Moon Landscape', a drawing by Petr Ginz, a boy killed in the Holocaust.

happened: During launch, a piece of foam broke off the external tank and struck Columbia's wing, damaging its thermal protection system.
Sixteen days later, as Columbia returned to Earth, the damaged wing let hot gases in during re-entry and the orbiter broke apart.
The Columbia Accident Investigation Board found both the physical cause and organisational causes, including accepting known risks as normal.
changed: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board made 29 recommendations, 15 of which NASA had to meet before the shuttle flew again.
The foam on the external tank was redesigned, and shuttles gained a boom with a laser scanner to inspect the heat shield in orbit.
Shuttle flights resumed with STS-114 on 26 July 2005, which included inspection of the orbiter's heat shield in orbit.
The shuttle program ended with its last flight, STS-135, in July 2011.
columbia.lesson: A known problem that goes unresolved can become a disaster, so unexpected damage must be investigated rather than accepted as normal.

quote.text: It is today that we remember and honor the crews of Apollo 1 and Challenger.
quote.by: Commander Rick Husband, aboard Columbia, 28 January 2003, four days before the accident

apollo1.vehicle: Apollo command module 012, on its launch pad
apollo1.place: Launch Complex 34, Cape Kennedy, Florida, during a ground test
apollo1.opening: On 27 January 1967, this happened to three real people.

crew.name: Virgil I. "Gus" Grissom
crew.line: One of the original Mercury Seven astronauts, he was the first American to fly in space twice.

crew.name: Edward H. White II
crew.line: He became the first American to walk in space on Gemini 4 in 1965, and as a young man ran the 400-metre hurdles and narrowly missed the 1952 US Olympic team.

crew.name: Roger B. Chaffee
crew.line: An Eagle Scout who loved hunting, woodworking and building models, he was preparing for his first spaceflight.

happened: The crew was taking part in a ground rehearsal of the launch, called a plugs-out test, about 25 days before their planned liftoff.
A fire started inside the cabin, which held pure oxygen at a pressure above sea level, and it spread too fast for them to escape.

The Apollo 204 Review Board found that the pure-oxygen atmosphere, combustible materials, wiring faults and a hatch that could not be opened quickly all contributed, and that the test had not been treated as hazardous.
changed: The three-piece hatch was replaced with a single hatch that opened outward in seconds.
NASA severely restricted and controlled the amount and location of combustible material in the spacecraft, and developed flame-resistant spacesuit materials.
Wiring was better protected, and NASA adopted a mixed-gas cabin atmosphere for Apollo instead of testing on the pad in pure oxygen.
The mission was renamed Apollo 1 in the crew's honour, and later crews flew the redesigned Block II spacecraft to the Moon.
apollo1.lesson: A test that looks routine can be deadly, so every test must be planned with the same care as a real flight.

quote.text: There will be risks, as there are in any experimental program, and sooner or later, we're going to run head-on into the law of averages and lose somebody.
quote.by: Gus Grissom, written shortly before his death, as quoted in NASA's biography of the Apollo 1 crew (cited there to his book Gemini)

soyuz11.place: high above the Earth, during the return from the Salyut 1 space station
soyuz11.opening: On 30 June 1971, this happened to three real people.

crew.name: Georgy Dobrovolsky
crew.line: A military pilot and parachutist, he commanded the first crew to live aboard a space station.

crew.name: Vladislav Volkov
crew.line: An aeronautical engineer, he was on his second spaceflight.

crew.name: Viktor Patsayev
crew.line: A mechanical engineer, he became the first person to celebrate a birthday in space, aboard Salyut 1.

happened: The crew had spent about 23 days aboard Salyut 1, the world's first space station, and were the only crew ever to live aboard it.
When their descent module separated from the rest of the spacecraft before re-entry, a pressure-equalisation valve opened by mistake and the cabin lost its air.
The crew were not wearing pressure suits, and they could not be revived after landing; they are the only people known to have died in space.
changed: Soyuz valves were redesigned and made more robust.
The spacecraft was reconfigured to carry two cosmonauts instead of three, so that both could wear pressure suits.
Pressure suits became standard for launch and re-entry on Soyuz flights.
soyuz11.lesson: Even a routine return home needs protection against a single failure, so crews must be given a safety margin at every stage of the flight.

sources.title: Astronomy magazine: Remembering the crew of Soyuz 11

closing.text: In August 1971 the crew of Apollo 15 left a small aluminium figure, 'Fallen Astronaut', on the Moon beside a plaque bearing the names of 14 astronauts and cosmonauts who had died. The exploration continues because of them.
